summary: This WhatIs.com definition explains the term harmonic, a wave or signal whose frequency is an integer multiple of a reference (fundamental) frequency. It covers harmonic series and even/odd harmonics, notes that most signals contain harmonic energy, and describes interference from harmonics in wireless broadcasting. It also briefly defines related meanings: harmonic distortion, simple harmonic motion, automotive harmonic balancers, the harmonic series in mathematics, and harmonics in electrical systems caused by nonlinear loads.
one_line: A definition of harmonics: waves whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of a fundamental frequency, plus related meanings in electronics, physics and engines.
key_facts: A harmonic is a wave or signal whose frequency is an integral (whole number) multiple of the frequency of the same reference signal or wave.
The fundamental frequency or original wave is known as the first, or 1st, harmonic.
For a signal whose fundamental frequency is f, the second harmonic has a frequency of 2f and the third harmonic has a frequency of 3f.
The second harmonic has a wavelength of w/2, and the third harmonic has a wavelength of w/3, where w is the wavelength of the signal in a specified medium.
Signals at frequencies of 2f, 4f, 6f and more are called even harmonics; signals at 3f, 5f and 7f are called odd harmonics.
If a signal contains all its energy at the fundamental frequency, it is a perfect sine wave; square, sawtooth and triangular waves contain large amounts of energy at harmonic frequencies.
A broadcast signal at 90.5 megahertz (MHz) in the standard FM band would have a second harmonic at 181 MHz, a third harmonic at 271.5 MHz and a fourth harmonic at 362 MHz.
Signal output at harmonic frequencies can cause interference with other communications or broadcasting protocols.
In electrical distribution systems, harmonic distortion is a standard voltage and current variation resulting from frequency changes, such as a deviation from typical sinusoidal variations.
In physics, simple harmonic motion represents repetitive back-and-forth movement through a central or equilibrium position.
In simple harmonic motion, the force that creates the motion is always directed to the central equilibrium position and is directly proportional to the distance from it.
In automobiles, a harmonic balancer connects to the engine crankshaft and helps reduce engine vibration; it is also called a crankshaft damper, torsional damper or vibration damper.
In mathematics, a harmonic series describes the divergent infinite series of overtones or harmonics in music.
Examples of nonlinear loads that generate electrical harmonics include battery chargers, personal computers, laser printers, variable speed motors and drives, and switch-mode power supplies (SMPS).
The article was written by Andrew Zola and was last updated in November 2021.
